title: Conjunctive queries: evaluation and static analysis
short: Conjunctive queries: evaluation and static analysis
lead: Evaluation complexity, canonical databases, containment, equivalence and minimisation.

sections.title: Evaluation and data complexity
sections.html:
Recap: syntax, matches and projected witnesses

A CQ is a head plus a conjunction of relational atoms; body-only variables are existential. A match fixes constants and sends every body atom to a database fact. Project the match to the head variables to obtain an answer tuple. The repeated London–Glasgow example again uses x=LGW,y=GLA,z=U2; all three airport/flight facts must match simultaneously.

This lecture asks about algorithms and static analysis of that same set-based, positive language. The recap animations re-establish the semantics before stating complexity results; they introduce neither negation nor SQL NULL.

PDF pp. 1–9

Combined complexity versus data complexity

CQ-Evaluation is the decision problem: given D,Q and tuple ā, is ā∈Q(D)? Membership avoids confusing the cost of deciding an answer with the unavoidable size of enumerating a possibly huge output. Combined complexity varies both D and Q; CQ-Evaluation is NP-complete. Data complexity fixes Q and varies D and ā; then evaluation is polynomial in database size. A polynomial whose exponent depends on a fixed query does not give a uniform polynomial bound when the query varies.

PDF pp. 10–12

sections.title: Why combined evaluation is NP-complete
sections.html:
NP membership by guess and verify

P problems have polynomial-time algorithms; NP admits polynomial-size certificates verifiable in polynomial time. NP does not mean “not polynomial,” and NP-complete does not prove P≠NP. For CQ membership, guess a value for each variable, fix constants, verify every image atom belongs to D and that the head maps to the requested tuple. The assignment is the certificate.

For 3COL, a certificate assigns one of three colours to each vertex; verify every edge has different endpoint colours. Guess-and-verify establishes NP membership, while a separate reduction establishes hardness.

PDF pp. 13–16

Reduction from colouring and fixed-query enumeration

Encode each graph vertex as a variable and each edge as an E atom in a Boolean CQ QG. Use the three-colour target K3: E contains every ordered pair of distinct colours and no self-loop. A homomorphism sends adjacent vertices to different colours, exactly a proper 3-colouring, so G is colourable iff QG matches this fixed target. For a directed relation representation, include both edge orientations in K3; the slide’s three-edge shorthand denotes the undirected triangle, not a directed cycle.

If a fixed Q has v variables and the active domain has d values, enumerate at most d^v assignments, checking all its finitely many atoms. Since v is fixed, this is polynomial data complexity. In the reduction QG grows with G, so the two results do not contradict each other.

PDF pp. 17–18

sections.title: Static questions and canonical databases
sections.html:
Three static-analysis questions

Satisfiability asks whether some database makes Q nonempty. Equivalence asks Q1(D)=Q2(D) for every D. Containment asks Q1(D)⊆Q2(D) for every D. Testing equality on one current instance cannot establish equivalence. Equivalence is mutual containment; static analysis justifies replacing a query independently of the current database contents.

PDF pp. 19–22

Canonical databases and satisfiability

Construct D[Q] by replacing each variable with its own fresh constant, distinct from existing constants, while preserving all repeated occurrences. For Q(x,y):-R(x,y),P(y,z,w),R(z,x), create R(cx,cy),P(cy,cz,cw),R(cz,cx). The mapping c is invertible on those fresh names.

The canonical assignment witnesses a result of Q on D[Q], proving every basic positive CQ is satisfiable. This assumes no external constraints or contradictory built-in predicates. For example, adding disequality x≠x would leave the basic language and break the claim. Containment can also be related to conjunction of aligned queries, with existential variables renamed apart.

PDF pp. 23–25

sections.title: Containment through homomorphisms
sections.html:
The reverse direction of containment mappings

A query homomorphism preserves body atoms and maps the ordered source head to the ordered target head. The theorem is Q1⊆Q2 iff a query homomorphism Q2→Q1 exists. The direction is easy to reverse by mistake: the less restrictive query maps into the more restrictive pattern.

Q1(x,y) :- R(x,z), S(z,z), R(z,y)
Q2(a,b) :- R(a,c), S(c,d), R(d,b)

h:a→x,b→y,c→z,d→z maps Q2 into Q1, proving Q1⊆Q2. No map Q1→Q2 can create its required S(t,t), because Q2 has only S(c,d) with distinct terms. On D[Q2], the output (ca,cb) satisfies Q2 but not Q1, witnessing strict containment.

PDF pp. 26–27

Both directions of the homomorphism theorem

Forward: assume Q1⊆Q2. The canonical head c(head1) is in Q1(D[Q1]), hence in Q2(D[Q1]). Its Q2 match h maps body2 into c(body1). Compose with c⁻¹ to obtain the required head-preserving map Q2→Q1.

Backward: given h:Q2→Q1, take any tuple t in Q1(D), witnessed by g:body1→D. Composition g∘h maps body2 to D and head2 to t. Therefore t is in Q2(D). Since D and t were arbitrary, Q1⊆Q2. The canonical construction handles necessity; composition handles sufficiency.

PDF pp. 28–29

Complexity of static analysis

Guessing a head-preserving atom map and checking it gives NP membership. CQ-Evaluation reduces to existence of such a map, giving hardness; the homomorphism theorem transfers it to containment. CQ containment and equivalence are NP-complete in the general combined setting, while satisfiability of basic positive CQs is trivial. Do not infer that testing a fixed small query against data is therefore NP-complete.

PDF pp. 30–31

sections.title: CQ minimisation and cores
sections.html:
Minimisation by deletion

A minimal CQ has no equivalent CQ with fewer atoms. The deletion theorem says an equivalent minimal pattern can be obtained from a subset of the original body. Try deleting an atom α while keeping every head variable in the remaining body. The reduced query has fewer constraints, so the original is automatically contained in it. To establish the other containment, find a head-preserving homomorphism from the original query into the reduced one. Repeat successful deletions until none remains. This is a semantic test, not a rule that any similar-looking atom is redundant.

PDF pp. 32–34

Worked deletion and the unique core

Q(x) :- R(x,y), R(x,b), R(a,b), R(u,c), R(u,v), S(a,c,d)

Here a,b,c,d are constants. Delete R(x,y) using y→b, because R(x,b) remains. Delete R(u,v) using v→c, because R(u,c) remains. Keep R(x,b),R(a,b),R(u,c),S(a,c,d). Mapping x→a is forbidden because the distinguished head must stay x; it cannot justify deleting R(x,b). The resulting four-atom query is minimal in the source example.

Different deletion orders may choose renamed forms, but all equivalent minimal CQs are isomorphic, preserving constants and output positions. This unique-up-to-renaming core reduces redundant joins without changing answers. The lecture closes by separating combined evaluation hardness, polynomial data complexity and static-analysis results.

PDF pp. 35–37

quiz.question: To prove Q1 ⊆ Q2 using the homomorphism theorem, which mapping should you seek?
options: Only compare the number of atoms
quiz.explanation: The mapping goes against the direction of containment and must preserve the head and the constants.

source.summary: Lecture 24 studies the complexity of conjunctive-query evaluation, canonical databases, satisfiability, containment and equivalence through homomorphisms, and minimization to a core.

limitations: These theoretical results apply to conjunctive queries under set semantics. They do not automatically apply to SQL bags, NULL values, or additional constraints.
